title: Baptists and free churches
hookLine: a believer's baptism, a local congregation, freedom of conscience

lines: A BOOK SENT TO THE KING.
YOU HAVE NO POWER OVER SOULS.
cards: London, 1612. Thomas Helwys has just come home from exile in Amsterdam, where he helped start one of the first Baptist congregations. He's written a little book, and does something bold.

He signs a copy and sends it to King James, the same King James whose name is on the well-known Bible. Helwys tells the king, more or less: you are a mortal man, not God. You have no power over people's souls.
Let them be heretics, Muslims, Jews or anything else: it isn't the king's business to punish anyone for what they believe. In 1612, that was almost unthinkable.
Helwys was thrown into prison, and died there a few years later.

teach.h: BAPTISM FOR THOSE WHO CHOOSE IT.
teach.b: Baptists began among English Christians in exile in Amsterdam in the early 1600s, around John Smyth and Thomas Helwys. They held three things close.
First, baptism is for believers: people old enough to say for themselves that they follow Christ.
They baptize by immersion, all the way under, and love Paul's picture of it: "we are buried with him by baptism into death," and raised to "walk in newness of life."
Other churches, Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, Reformed, Methodist, baptize infants too, seeing baptism as God's gift before a child can ask for it.
Both sides have scripture they cherish, and the conversation goes on. Second, the local congregation. Each Baptist church governs itself, no bishop or king above it.
That's what free church means: free from the state, free to call its own pastor. Many others share that shape: Congregationalists, Churches of Christ, countless independent churches.

teach.h: SOUL FREEDOM: FAITH CAN'T BE FORCED.
teach.b: Third, freedom of conscience, which Baptists sometimes call soul freedom or soul liberty. Faith has to be chosen freely, or it isn't faith.
Roger Williams, who founded Providence, in what became Rhode Island, in 1636, built a colony on it and helped start a Baptist church there, remembered as the first in America.

Baptists pushed hard for the separation of church and state in the new United States. Black Baptist churches were at the heart of the civil rights movement: Martin Luther King Jr. was a Baptist pastor.
From a book sent to a king in 1612 to a pulpit in Montgomery, one idea: nobody can believe for you.

how: Baptist churches baptize believers by immersion, often in a pool at the front of the church, each congregation calls its own pastor, and worship centers on preaching, singing and prayer.

games.q: it's 1612. you believe no king has power over anyone's soul. the king is James, and he doesn't agree. what do you do?
o: write a book saying so, sign it, and send it to the king.
games.why: Thomas Helwys sent his book to King James. he was imprisoned and died a few years later, but the idea outlived him.

practice: Think of what you believe, or don't, and notice you're free to hold it, free to question it, free to be right here learning; many in history weren't, and some still aren't.
If you pray, thank God for freedom of conscience and pray for those in prison for what they believe; if not, feel grateful, and hold those people in mind.
